entry.header: What kind of earner are you?
entry.subhead: Income doesn't fit into two neat boxes. Find where you fit, and see how the tax system actually sees you.

w2.title: I'm a W-2 employee
w2.subtitle: I get a paycheck with taxes already taken out.

freelance.title: I do freelance or contract work
freelance.subtitle: I'm paid directly by clients, customers, or platforms.

mixed.title: I have a job AND side income
mixed.subtitle: I'm an employee, but I also earn on the side.

investment.title: I have investment, interest, or retirement income
investment.subtitle: Money comes from accounts, not from work.

pathA.header: Your income follows a straightforward path
pathA.intro: W-2 income follows a straightforward path through the payroll system. Taxes are withheld along the way, and the results are reported on Form W-2 at year-end.
pathA.introItalic: Most of your tax is handled before you file. Your employer withholds, deposits with the IRS, and reports the totals on your W-2. Filing reconciles the math.

confusion.title: Understanding refunds
confusion.body: A refund doesn't mean you didn't pay tax. It means you
confusion.bodyEnd: through the year and the IRS is returning the difference.

paycheck.title: You receive a paycheck
paycheck.detail: Payroll system processes your pay and withholds taxes automatically.

w2Form.title: Form W-2
w2Form.desc: Generally issued by January 31 of the following year

reconciliation.title: Reconciliation happens
reconciliation.subtitle: The IRS compares what was withheld against what you owe
reconciliation.refundDesc: More was withheld than you owed
reconciliation.balanceDueDesc: Not enough was withheld during the year

complicated.title: When this gets more complicated
complicated.body: If you also have side income, your W-2 withholding usually isn't enough to cover the tax on that side income.

insight.title: What makes W-2 different
insight.content: Your employer acts as a tax collector. They calculate, withhold, and remit taxes on your behalf. You don't make estimated payments. Self-employment tax doesn't apply. Your responsibility begins when you file.

compare.prompt: Curious how this compares to other income types?

pathB.header: You're now responsible for your own taxes
pathB.intro: When you're paid directly by clients without an employer intermediary, the tax responsibilities shift entirely to you.

client.title: Client / Customer / Platform
client.desc: A person or business pays you for your work

directPayment.title: You're paid directly
directPayment.desc: Deposit, transfer, check, cash, or app payout
directPayment.noWithholding: No withholding. Gross payment arrives in your account.

flow.keyInsight: When you're paid directly, nothing is withheld. The income arrives gross. The responsibility for tax—and the timing of paying it—moves to you.

forms.title: Form you may receive
forms.desc: By January 31 of the following year
forms.necDesc: Clients generally issue this form when payments reach $600 or more.
forms.kNote: The form reports payment volume — not automatically taxable income.
forms.stillReportDesc: Income is taxable whether you receive a form or not.

scheduleC.title: Schedule C
scheduleC.desc: Profit or Loss From Business (Sole Proprietorship)

schedule1.title: Schedule 1 → Form 1040
schedule1.desc: Net profit adds to your total income

twoTaxes.title: Two taxes apply to net profit
twoTaxes.subtitle: This is the key difference from W-2 income
twoTaxes.incomeTaxBody: Same tax that applies to W-2 wages. Rate depends on your bracket and filing status.
twoTaxes.seTaxBody: Both halves of Social Security (12.4%) and Medicare (2.9%). W-2 employees split this with their employer.

quarterly.title: Nothing was withheld for taxes
quarterly.desc: You may need to pay quarterly estimated tax — here's when that rule applies.

q1.title: "If I didn't receive a 1099, do I have to report the income?"
q1.yesDetail: The 1099 is a copy sent to you and the IRS. It's not what creates the obligation to report.
q1.note: You're required to report all income regardless of whether you received a form.

q2.title: "Is 1099 income the same as Schedule C income?"
q2.notAlwaysDetail: 1099-NEC and most 1099-K income land on Schedule C. Other 1099 forms don't.

quietBridge.title: The quiet bridge
quietBridge.body: Many people don't realize when "a little side work" has quietly become "a small business." Schedule C is where that line becomes visible.

insight.title: The key shift
insight.content: You became your own payroll department. No employer to withhold for you. The responsibility—and the timing—changed. You may need to pay estimated taxes quarterly to avoid penalties.

explore1099.prompt: Want to understand the different 1099 forms?

pathC.intro: This is increasingly common. You have a job with a W-2 and also earn money independently. Your tax return reflects both—and the side income can change your outcome.

flow.bothLandDesc: W-2 wages + Schedule C net profit combined

scheduleC.title: Schedule C
scheduleC.desc: Report income, expenses, calculate net profit

surprise.title: Withholding from W-2 may not be enough
surprise.body: Your job's withholding was set for your W-2 income alone. Side income brings additional tax—with no withholding to cover it.
surprise.tagLine: This is why "I had a job AND a side gig"
surprise.result: can produce a surprise balance due

refundGone.title: "My refund disappeared"
refundGone.body: If you had a refund before you started a side gig—and now you don't—this is usually why. The W-2 side hasn't changed. The side income brought its own taxes.

solutions.title: Two valid approaches

w4.title: Adjust W-4
w4.body: Increase withholding from your paycheck to cover side income tax too. One change, no extra forms. Set it and forget it.

quarterly.title: Quarterly payments
quarterly.body: Make estimated tax payments on your side income using Form 1040-ES. More bookkeeping, but keeps side and job separate.

solutions.bothValid: Both are valid. Both prevent surprises.

insight.title: You're running two tax profiles
insight.content: The W-2 side is handled for you. The side-income side requires your attention. They meet on one 1040. Many people in this situation underwithhold because they don't account for self-employment tax on side income.

pathD.header: Investment & retirement income has its own forms
pathD.intro: When money comes from accounts—not from work—a different family of 1099s reports it. These are not self-employment. No Schedule C.

receive.title: You receive...
receive.desc: Distribution, interest, dividend, or proceeds from a sale

flow.formsSubtitle: Each type of income has its own 1099
flow.passive: These forms report investment and account income—money from accounts, not from your work. No self-employment tax. No quarterly payments needed.

insight.title: The important distinction
insight.content: These 1099s report investment and account income—interest, dividends, capital gains, retirement. They are NOT the same as 1099-NEC which reports self-employment income. Different forms. Different lines on your return. Different tax treatment.

pathD.confused: Confused by all the 1099s? You're not alone.

family1099.intro: "1099" is a family of information returns, not a single form. Each reports different types of income and lands on different parts of your return.

nec.description: Reports payments to contractors, freelancers, and non-employees. This is the modern form for what used to be Box 7 of 1099-MISC.

k.fullName: Payment Card and Third Party Network Transactions
k.description: Reports payments received through payment apps (Venmo, PayPal) and platforms. Thresholds are changing.
k.landingSpot: Often Schedule C. Sometimes just gross receipts.
k.taxNotes: May indicate self-employment income. Context matters.

misc.description: Reports rents, royalties, prizes, awards, medical payments, and other income types. Box 7 used to be for self-employment—that moved to 1099-NEC.
misc.landingSpot: Depends on box. Rents → Schedule E. Royalties → Schedule E.
misc.taxNotes: Not all 1099-MISC = Schedule C. Box matters.

g.description: Reports government payments including unemployment compensation, state and local tax refunds, and other government payments such as agricultural payments.
g.landingSpot: Form 1040, Schedule 1 (unemployment). State refunds on Schedule 1 if previously deducted.
g.taxNotes: Unemployment is fully taxable as ordinary income. State tax refunds are taxable only if you deducted state taxes in the prior year.

int.description: Bank interest, savings bonds, loans you made.
int.taxNotes: Ordinary income tax. No self-employment tax.

div.taxNotes: Qualified dividends have lower tax rates.

b.description: Stock, bond, mutual fund sales. Also crypto from some platforms.
b.taxNotes: Capital gains tax. Short-term vs long-term.

r.description: 401(k), IRA, pension, and other retirement plan distributions.
r.taxNotes: May be taxable, partially taxable, or nontaxable.

sidePanel.selectPrompt: Select a form to see details

insight.title: The biggest misconception
insight.content: 'I got a 1099, so I'm self-employed.' Not necessarily. 1099-INT, 1099-DIV, 1099-B, and 1099-R report investment and account income—not self-employment. Only certain 1099s connect to Schedule C.

scheduleCView.header: The quiet bridge between side work and business
scheduleCView.intro: Schedule C is where the IRS asks you to describe your profit-seeking activity. It's where "I do some work on the side" becomes visible as a business.

what.title: What is Schedule C?
what.body: Schedule C is "Profit or Loss From Business (Sole Proprietorship)." It's a form where you report:
items: All income from your self-employment or freelance work
All ordinary and necessary business expenses
The resulting net profit or loss
what.footer: The net profit flows to your Form 1040 as income.

when.title: When does Schedule C appear?
items: You're a single-member LLC taxed as a disregarded entity
You have a side business or gig work
when.footer: Income type matters more than amount. If you earned $600 doing freelance graphic design, that's Schedule C. If you earned $600 in stock dividends, that's not Schedule C.

line.title: The line between side income and business
line.body: From a tax perspective, there isn't a bright line. The IRS looks at whether you're:
items: Operating with a profit motive (not just a hobby)
Engaged in the activity regularly and continuously
line.footer: You don't need an LLC, registered business name, or separate bank account to have Schedule C income. The form is filed based on how you earned the money, not how you're organized.

expenses.title: What expenses can you deduct?
expenses.body: Ordinary and necessary business expenses. Common examples:
items: Software, subscriptions, tools for your work
expenses.footer: Record-keeping matters. The IRS can disallow deductions without documentation.

selfemp.title: Self-employment tax
selfemp.body: When you have Schedule C net profit, Schedule SE follows. This is where you calculate:
selfemp.footer: As an employee, your employer paid half. When you're self-employed, you pay both halves—but you can deduct half on your 1040.

insight.title: Schedule C is descriptive, not prescriptive
insight.content: It doesn't create a business. It reports one that already exists because of how you're earning. You don't opt into Schedule C—the nature of your income determines whether it applies.

comparison.intro: Imagine the same person doing the same kind of work, earning the same $100,000—but arranged three different ways. The tax system treats each arrangement differently, and what reaches you at the end can be very different.

employed.title: Employed at a firm
employed.notes: Employer pays the other half of FICA (7.65%). Benefits paid by employer. No Schedule C.
structure: Employer covers half of Social Security & Medicare

contracted.title: Contracted as hired expert
contracted.notes: You pay both halves of FICA. No employer benefits. Quarterly estimated payments may apply.
structure: You cover your own tools & software
You pay full SE tax (no split)

solo.title: Solo practice / small business
solo.notes: Real business overhead. You deduct the actual cost of running it. Quarterly payments likely.

rows.businessExpensesNote2: office, software, insurance, marketing, supplies, CE

employed: Employer covers half of FICA taxes
contracted: You pay full SE tax (no employer split)
No withholding; you manage tax timing
solo: Real overhead: office, software, insurance, marketing
You deduct actual costs of running it
You pay full SE tax and manage quarterly payments

realDifference.title: The real difference
realDifference.body1: Columns 2 and 3 use the same tax forms (1099, Schedule C, Schedule SE). The difference isn't the tax rules. It's the
realDifference.body2: A contracted expert usually has minimal overhead. A solo practice or small business—whether you offer services, sell goods, or run an operation—has the costs of actually running it: workspace, tools, insurance, marketing, dues, supplies.

disclaimer.label: All numbers are illustrative.
disclaimer.body1: Real outcomes depend on your filing status, state, family situation, actual expenses, pre-tax contributions, credits, and many other factors.
disclaimer.body2: This is a conceptual comparison of how the same gross income is treated under three structures—not a calculator, and not a recommendation for which structure is "best" for you. Each has legitimate use cases. The structure you choose changes what you can deduct, which changes what gets taxed, which changes what reaches you.

raiseCalc.subtitle: Sometimes a raise feels smaller than it looks. People often hear "I moved into the 22% bracket" and assume all their income is taxed at that rate. It's not how brackets work.
raiseCalc.bracketsHeader: How your income moves through brackets
raiseCalc.marginalRateNote: This is the bracket people talk about
raiseCalc.effectiveRateNote: Federal income tax only (total tax ÷ gross salary)
raiseCalc.whyDiffBody: You don't pay 22% on your entire salary. Most of it is in lower brackets. Only the money above the $48,475 threshold is taxed at 22%.
raiseCalc.keptPercent: About {{pct}}% of your raise remained after federal income tax.
raiseCalc.disclaimer: This shows federal income tax only for 2025 tax year estimates. It excludes FICA (7.65%), state tax, pre-tax deductions, and credits. Your actual take-home will be lower.

quarterly.thresholdBody: Quarterly payments are generally required if you expect to still owe the IRS $1,000 or more at filing time — after withholding and refundable credits.
quarterly.thresholdNote: The $1,000 is not your total tax. It's what's still owed after everything already paid in.
quarterly.safeHarborIntro: Even if you'll owe more than $1,000, you generally avoid an underpayment penalty if your withholding plus estimated payments cover at least:
quarterly.safeHarborNote: (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000, or $75,000 if married filing separately)
quarterly.safeHarborSmaller: Meeting either safe harbor generally avoids the penalty.
quarterly.safeHarborW2Note: This is why people with stable W-2 jobs and small side income often don't need separate quarterly payments — their W-2 withholding can be enough to satisfy the safe harbor on its own.
quarterly.confusionQ: "My total tax will be way more than $1,000. Do I need to pay quarterly?"
quarterly.confusionA: Not necessarily. The $1,000 threshold is about what's still owed
quarterly.confusionAEnd: . If your W-2 withholding already covers most of your tax, you may be fine even with significant side income.
quarterly.disclaimer: Simplified for clarity. Actual requirements depend on your full picture: withholding, credits, prior-year tax, and safe harbor rules.

box1.label: Wages, tips, other compensation
box1.desc: Your taxable wages — gross pay reduced by 401(k), HSA, and pre-tax health insurance.

box2.label: Federal income tax withheld
box2.desc: Federal income tax already paid to the IRS on your behalf. Counts against what you owe at filing.

box3.label: Social Security wages
box3.desc: Wages subject to Social Security tax. Usually equals gross pay minus pre-tax health insurance. 401(k) does NOT reduce this.

box4.label: Social Security tax withheld
box4.desc: Social Security tax already withheld — your half of the 12.4% SS tax (6.2% of Box 3).

box5.label: Medicare wages and tips
box5.desc: Wages subject to Medicare tax. Like Box 3, but no wage cap applies.

box6.label: Medicare tax withheld
box6.desc: Medicare tax already withheld — your half of the 2.9% Medicare tax (1.45% of Box 5).

box17.label: State income tax
box17.desc: State income tax already withheld and remitted by your employer.
box17.where: Your state tax return — state tax withheld line

box1.label: Nonemployee compensation
box1.desc: Gross amount paid to you for services. Your client sends this when they paid you $600 or more during the year — it arrives by January 31. This number goes directly to Schedule C, Part I, Line 1 as gross receipts before any expense deductions.
box1.where: Schedule C, Part I, Line 1 (gross receipts or sales)

box4.label: Federal income tax withheld
box4.desc: Backup withholding — nearly always $0 for 1099-NEC. You receive the full payment amount and are responsible for estimating and paying your own taxes quarterly. If you see a non-zero amount here, it means your tax ID was flagged for backup withholding.
box4.where: Form 1040, Line 25a (federal tax withheld) — offsets what you owe at filing

box5.label: State tax withheld
box5.desc: State income tax withheld by the payer, if any. Nearly always $0 — self-employed workers are responsible for paying their own state estimated taxes.
box5.where: Your state income tax return — state tax withheld line

box6.label: State / Payer's state no.
box6.desc: The state where the income was earned and the payer's state tax ID number. Used to match the income to the correct state filing jurisdiction.
box6.where: State return — identifies the filing state

box7.label: State income
box7.desc: The amount of compensation attributable to the state listed in Box 6. Usually equals Box 1 if you work in a single state.
box7.where: State income tax return — same figure as Box 1 in single-state situations

box1a.label: Gross amount of payment card/third party network transactions
box1a.desc: Total gross receipts reported to the IRS — this is before platform fees, refunds, chargebacks, or any deductions. Your actual taxable amount on Schedule C will usually be lower: you deduct platform fees and other expenses in Part II. Do not assume Box 1a equals your profit.
box1a.where: Schedule C, Part I, Line 1 (gross receipts) — then deduct fees and refunds as expenses in Part II

box4.label: Federal income tax withheld
box4.desc: Backup withholding — nearly always $0. You are responsible for paying your own taxes through quarterly estimated payments (April 15, June 16, Sept 15, Jan 15 of the following year).
box4.where: Form 1040, Line 25a — offsets what you owe at filing

box5a.label: January transactions
box5a.desc: Gross payment volume processed in January. Boxes 5a–5l break down the annual Box 1a total by month — useful for estimating quarterly tax payments.
box5a.where: Reference — the 12-month total (5a through 5l) equals Box 1a

box5b.label: February transactions
box5b.desc: Gross payment volume processed in February.

box5c.label: March transactions
box5c.desc: Gross payment volume for March. Q1 total (5a + 5b + 5c) helps you estimate how much to pay by April 15 for your first quarterly payment.

scheduleC.formTitle: Schedule C · Profit or Loss From Business
scheduleC.hoverPrompt: Hover or focus any line to see what it reports and where it lands.

line1.label: Gross receipts or sales
line1.desc: Total income received from your business before any deductions. Includes all 1099-NEC amounts, 1099-K amounts, direct payments, and any other business revenue — whether or not you received a form.
line1.where: Starting point for Schedule C income. Platform fees and refunds are deducted as Part II expenses.

line7.label: Gross income
line7.desc: Gross receipts minus cost of goods sold (if applicable). For most service-based freelancers, this equals Line 1 — cost of goods sold only applies if you sell physical products.
line7.where: Carries into Part II as the income figure against which expenses are subtracted.

line8.label: Advertising
line8.desc: Business promotion costs — website hosting, paid ads, business cards, social media promotion, print materials. Must be ordinary and necessary for the business.
line8.where: Part II total → subtracted from Line 7 to reach net profit on Line 31.

line18.label: Office expense
line18.desc: Office supplies used directly in your business — printer paper, pens, folders, toner. Separate from home office (Line 30) and from equipment over $2,500 (which may need depreciation).
line18.where: Part II total → subtracted from Line 7 to reach net profit on Line 31.

line22.label: Supplies
line22.desc: Materials and supplies used in delivering your service — tools, client materials, project-specific purchases. The line between Line 18 and Line 22 is fuzzy; the IRS cares more that you claim it somewhere than exactly which line.
line22.where: Part II total → subtracted from Line 7 to reach net profit on Line 31.

line25.label: Utilities
line25.desc: Business-portion utility costs — phone (business use percentage), internet (business use percentage), electricity for a dedicated home office. You may need to allocate based on square footage or usage.
line25.where: Part II total → subtracted from Line 7 to reach net profit on Line 31.

line27a.label: Other expenses
line27a.desc: Ordinary and necessary business expenses not listed on Lines 8–26 — software subscriptions, professional dues, continuing education, bank fees, business books, reference materials.
line27a.where: Part II total → subtracted from Line 7 to reach net profit on Line 31.

line28.label: Total expenses
line28.desc: Sum of all business expenses from Lines 8 through 27b. This is the total deductible amount against your gross income — every dollar here reduces your taxable profit.
line28.where: Subtracted from Line 7 (gross income) to calculate net profit on Line 31.

line31.label: Net profit or (loss)
line31.desc: Your business bottom line — gross income minus total expenses. This single number does two things: it flows to Schedule 1 as ordinary income (subject to income tax), and it also becomes the base for Schedule SE (self-employment tax). Every dollar of legitimate expense reduces both taxes simultaneously.
line31.where: Schedule 1, Line 3 → Form 1040, Line 8 (ordinary income). Also base for Schedule SE self-employment tax.

net.label: Net SE earnings
net.desc: Your net profit from Schedule C — gross receipts minus all allowable business expenses. This is the starting number for the entire self-employment tax calculation.
net.where: Schedule SE, Line 2 or Line 3 (depending on method)

adjustment.desc: Multiply net earnings by 92.35% (that is, 100% minus 7.65%). This removes the employer-equivalent half of SE tax from the taxable base — mirroring how W-2 employees are not taxed on the employer share of FICA that their employer pays on their behalf.
adjustment.where: Schedule SE, Line 4a — this becomes your SE income subject to tax

rate.desc: This is the combined employee AND employer share of FICA. A W-2 employee pays 7.65% and their employer quietly pays the other 7.65% — but as self-employed you pay both halves yourself. The rate applies to the 92.35%-adjusted amount, not your full net profit.
rate.where: Schedule SE, Line 12 (SS) + Line 13 (Medicare) = Line 15 total → Form 1040 Schedule 2, Line 4

deductible.label: ÷ 2 = Deductible half
deductible.desc: Half of your SE tax is deductible as an above-the-line adjustment on Schedule 1. This partially compensates for paying both halves of FICA — it reduces your adjusted gross income and therefore your income tax base, even though the SE tax itself is still fully owed.
deductible.where: Schedule 1, Line 15 → reduces Form 1040 adjusted gross income before the standard deduction

box1.label: Interest income
box1.desc: Total taxable interest earned from bank accounts, savings accounts, CDs, and bonds. If your total interest income from all sources is $1,500 or less, you can report it directly on Form 1040. If over $1,500, you must also complete Schedule B.
box1.where: Schedule B, Part I → Form 1040, Line 2b (taxable interest)

box2.label: Early withdrawal penalty
box2.desc: Penalty you paid for withdrawing from a time deposit (like a CD) before maturity. Even though it reduces your actual return, you still report the full interest in Box 1 — then deduct this penalty separately as an above-the-line adjustment.
box2.where: Schedule 1, Line 18 (Penalty on early withdrawal of savings) — reduces your AGI

box3.label: Interest on U.S. Savings Bonds and Treasury obligations
box3.desc: Interest from federal government securities — U.S. Savings Bonds (like Series EE or I), Treasury bills, notes, and bonds. This interest is exempt from state and local income tax, but is fully taxable for federal purposes.
box3.where: Form 1040, Line 2b (federal) — exempt from state return

box4.label: Federal income tax withheld
box4.desc: Backup withholding applied if your tax ID was missing or flagged. Rare for most bank accounts — but if you see a non-zero amount, it means the bank has already sent that money to the IRS on your behalf.
box4.where: Form 1040, Line 25a (federal tax withheld) — reduces what you owe at filing

box1a.label: Total ordinary dividends
box1a.desc: All dividends received from stocks and mutual funds. This is your total dividend income — but not all of it is taxed the same way. Box 1b (below) shows the portion that qualifies for lower rates.
box1a.where: Schedule B, Part II (if over $1,500 total) → Form 1040, Line 3b

box1b.label: Qualified dividends
box1b.desc: The most misunderstood box on this form. Qualified dividends are a subset of Box 1a — they come from U.S. corporations (or qualifying foreign ones) and you held the stock long enough. They are taxed at preferential long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15%, or 20%) instead of your ordinary income tax rate. A dividend is not automatically qualified just because a company declared it.
box1b.where: Form 1040, Line 3a — taxed at capital gains rates, not ordinary income rates

box2a.label: Total capital gain distributions
box2a.desc: Gains distributed by mutual funds and ETFs from selling securities inside the fund during the year. You receive this even if you never sold your fund shares. Treated as long-term capital gain regardless of how long you held the fund.
box2a.where: Schedule D, Part II (long-term) → Form 1040, Line 13

box4.label: Federal income tax withheld
box4.desc: Backup withholding on dividends — rare for most investors. If non-zero, the brokerage sent this amount directly to the IRS and it counts as a tax payment you already made.
box4.where: Form 1040, Line 25a (federal tax withheld) — offsets what you owe

box1a.label: Description of property
box1a.desc: What was sold — typically the security name and number of shares, units of crypto, or description of property.
box1a.where: Schedule D, Part I or Part II (description column)

box1c.label: Date sold or disposed
box1c.desc: The date of the sale. Combined with the purchase date, this determines whether the gain or loss is short-term (held 1 year or less) or long-term (held more than 1 year).
box1c.where: Schedule D — determines which section (short vs. long-term) and applicable tax rate

box1d.label: Proceeds
box1d.desc: The amount you received from the sale — your gross selling price. Gain or loss = Proceeds (Box 1d) minus Basis (Box 1e). If Box 1e is blank, you must determine your own cost basis.
box1d.where: Schedule D, Proceeds column → Form 8949 if adjustments needed

box1e.label: Cost or other basis
box1e.desc: What you originally paid for the asset (purchase price + commissions). If this box is blank or shows $0, the broker did not have basis information on file — you must look up your original purchase price and report the correct basis yourself.
box1e.where: Schedule D, Cost/Basis column — subtracted from Box 1d to get your gain or loss

box2.label: Type of gain or loss
box2.desc: Short-term = held 1 year or less → taxed at ordinary income rates. Long-term = held more than 1 year → taxed at preferential capital gains rates (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).
box2.where: Schedule D, Part I (short-term) or Part II (long-term)

box1.label: Gross distribution
box1.desc: Total amount distributed from your retirement account before any withholding or taxes. This is the full amount that left the account.
box1.where: Form 1040, Line 5a (pension/annuity total) — Box 2a is the taxable portion

box2a.label: Taxable amount
box2a.desc: The portion of the distribution subject to income tax. Usually equals Box 1 for traditional 401(k) and IRA distributions. May be less than Box 1 if you made after-tax (non-deductible) contributions.
box2a.where: Form 1040, Line 5b (pension/annuity taxable amount) → added to ordinary income

box4.label: Federal income tax withheld
box4.desc: Federal income tax withheld from your distribution — typically 20% for most retirement plan withdrawals, or 10% for IRA distributions (both are adjustable). This counts as a payment toward your tax bill.
box4.where: Form 1040, Line 25b (federal tax withheld) — reduces what you owe at filing

box7.label: Distribution code(s)
box7.desc: The most important box on the form — even though it is just a letter or number. Code 1 = early distribution (under 59½), may trigger 10% penalty. Code 2 = early, exception applies. Code 7 = normal distribution (59½ or older). Code G = direct rollover (not taxable). The code determines whether you owe a penalty.
box7.where: Determines Form 5329 (additional taxes) — penalty applies if Code 1 with no exception
